summary: This program builds a list of Song objects and then sorts it three times — by title, by energy level from highest to lowest, and by artist — printing the playlist after each sort. It shows how Comparator lets you order the same list by different fields without writing your own sorting code.

lines.text: Comparator is the interface that describes how to compare two objects; its static helper methods build the orderings used further down.
The variable is declared as List but created as an ArrayList, so the code depends only on the general list behaviour while getting the array-backed implementation.
Each add call appends one Song to the end of the list, so the starting order is the order the songs were added.
The enhanced for loop walks through every song in the list without you having to manage an index.
Passing an object to println calls its toString method, which is why the Song class needs a readable one.
Comparator.comparing takes a method that pulls out a value to compare — here the title — and sort rearranges the list in place using it.
forEach with a method reference is a compact alternative to the for loop above; each song is handed to println in turn.
comparingInt is the version of comparing for int values, which avoids wrapping each number in an Integer object.
reversed flips the comparator, turning the natural low-to-high number order into high-to-low.
Sorting again discards the previous ordering: the list keeps only whatever arrangement the most recent sort produced.
